middle_heading: Before you invest in your brand
middle_body: A strong name is only valuable if you can use it, protect it, and grow with it.\n\nTrademark planning helps founders avoid preventable rebrands, filing mistakes, and ownership problems before they become expensive.

Choosing and clearing a brand name

Understanding federal trademark filings

Identifying the right owner and filing strategy

Avoiding common mistakes that weaken protection

For founders, creators, consumer brands, software companies, and growing businesses preparing to launch or expand.\n\nUse the guide as a practical starting point before investing further in a name, product, or brand identity.
The supplied U.S. filings by Ate My Heart Inc. — the California company behind Lady Gaga’s trademarks — span 65 records and 18 distinct marks. The stage name is only the center of the map.

Her fan community became a brand asset. LITTLE MONSTERS earned four federal registrations in 2013 covering social networking, streaming, and online entertainment. Those registrations have since left the register — but the lesson stands: communities can be brand assets too.

Beauty is the busiest corner of the portfolio: live HAUS LABS registrations for cosmetics — the newest issued in 2025 — plus earlier fragrance filings like EAU DE GAGA, BAD ROMANCE, and LADY GAGA FAME that mapped the ambition years ahead.

Even characters got filings. JO CALDERONE — the male alter ego — drew seven intent-to-use applications in a single day in 2011, and MISS ASIA KINNEY covered pet-care products. Neither set was completed, but the instinct is pure brand architecture.

Albums, tours, and even a song became filings: ARTPOP and THE ARTPOP BALL covered merchandise and entertainment, GRIGIO GIRLS was filed for wine — and a GAGA registration for wines is still live today.
A valuable brand is rarely one name. It is a portfolio — the core mark, the products, the community, the personas, the campaigns — each protected on its own timeline. Map your brand universe early.

The supplied records break down cleanly: 9 live registrations, 4 pending intent-to-use applications, and 52 records no longer active. That ratio shows what an actively managed trademark portfolio looks like.

LADY GAGA was registered for entertainment services in 2009 from a 2008 filing, then for clothing, then recordings. By 2017, one merchandise registration spanned 14 classes. The core name came first — then kept deepening.

These records touch 21 international classes: cosmetics, clothing, entertainment, streaming, jewelry, even wine. Each class is a separate scope of protection. Coverage is a choice you design, not something registration hands you automatically.

All four live pending applications — HAUS LABS lines and a LADY GAGA cosmetics-accessory filing — were filed on an intent-to-use basis, reserving priority before products ship. Filing early is a strategy, not a formality.

HAUS BEAUTY and an early HAUS LABS application lapsed; refiled versions registered in 2022 and 2025. A 2015 HAUS LABORATORIES registration ended — a 2022 one is live. Portfolios get pruned and replanted as plans mature.

The playbook in these records scales to any company: register the core early, add categories as commerce follows, use intent-to-use filings to hold the runway, and let filings that no longer serve the plan go.

Among the supplied records, 42 applications are abandoned — including famous names like BAD ROMANCE and EAU DE GAGA. Abandoned has a narrow meaning: the application ended before registration. On its own, that is all it says.

Every one of those abandoned applications was filed on an intent-to-use basis — a placeholder for a plan. An intent-to-use filing only matures into a registration once real commercial use is proven. Many plans change first.

The record shows an application ended — never why. A statement of use goes unfiled, a deadline passes, plans shift, or a filing is replaced by a better one. None of that is visible from the status line.

Sixteen HAUS OF GAGA applications filed in a single day in 2011 went abandoned. Years later, HAUS LABS registrations issued and are live. An abandoned filing is often the rough draft of a sharper one.

BAD ROMANCE’s fragrance application is abandoned — the name is plainly not up for grabs. Common-law use, related live registrations, and other rights can survive an abandoned application. Availability takes a full search, not one status.

Filing? Calendar every deadline — abandonment is usually procedural, and extensions exist. Searching? Treat an abandoned application as the start of a question, never as clearance to adopt the name yourself.

Dead is a database label, not a single event. Of the 52 inactive records supplied, 42 are applications that never registered, and 10 are registrations that issued — and later left the register. The difference matters.

An application that ends before registration is abandoned. HAUS OF GAGA, JO CALDERONE, and GRIGIO GIRLS filings ended this way — intent-to-use claims that were never perfected, not registrations that were lost.

Registration is not permanent. LITTLE MONSTERS registered in 2013 for streaming and social networking; ARTPOP merchandise registered in 2015. All later left the register — registrations need ongoing maintenance filings to stay alive.

One HAUS LABORATORIES registration from 2015 is dead. Another HAUS LABORATORIES registration, issued in 2022, is live. A single dead record tells you almost nothing until you read the portfolio around it.
Eras end and products relaunch. Campaign marks like THE ARTPOP BALL come and go while the core LADY GAGA registrations stay live. In a working portfolio, that churn is health — not decay.

A dead federal record answers one narrow question. It cannot tell you whether use continues, common-law rights persist, or a related live filing exists. Never treat a dead-record search as a clearance opinion.
